content.title: About
content.content: Cornmeal mush with added fat is a traditional dish made from fine or medium‑ground cornmeal cooked with fat (oil, melted butter, or rendered pork fat). The resulting porridge is thick, creamy, mildly sweet, and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornmeal mush is one of the oldest staple foods of Indigenous peoples in North and South America.
Adding fat increases caloric density and makes the dish more satiating, which was important in cold climates and during heavy labor.
Different regions use different fats: butter is common in the United States, while rendered pork fat is traditional in many Eastern European cuisines.
Cornmeal provides carbohydrates, while the added fat supplies long‑lasting energy.
Historically the mush was cooked to a thick consistency that could be stored in a cool place for several days.

items.title: High energy content
items.content: The combination of cornmeal carbohydrates and added fat delivers both quick and sustained energy.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Cornmeal contains thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), which support carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The porridge provides dietary fiber that helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Essential fatty acids
items.content: The added fat supplies essential fatty acids and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Cornmeal contains zinc and iron, nutrients that contribute to a healthy immune system.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of the added fat, the dish is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn products, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oil is used, trans fats may be present, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: When salty fats such as rendered pork fat are used, the sodium content can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cornmeal mush hot, stirring in butter, rendered pork fat, or vegetable oil. Season to taste with salt, sugar, honey, or dried fruit. It can be eaten on its own or paired with meat or vegetable side dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry cornmeal in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Refrigerate cooked mush and consume within 2–3 days; reheat to a rolling boil before serving.
